sections.h2: Which Dawson County offices handle my property tax?
sections.html:
Dawson County runs property tax through two departments in the same building. The Tax Assessor sets values and receives exemption forms. The Tax Commissioner bills, collects and disburses all taxes under Georgia law, and also acts as the state's motor vehicle tag and title agent.

The commissioner is at 25 Justice Way, Suite 1222, inside the courthouse in downtown Dawsonville, reachable at (706) 344-3520 on weekdays between eight and five. The office runs its own site at dawsoncountytax.com and takes property tax payments by phone at (706) 701-2576. The assessor is down the hall at Suite 1201, on (706) 344-3590, and keeps a separate website with a property search, a sales search and a tax estimator.

Ask the Dawson County tax commissioner for the due date that applies to your parcel.

sections.h2: What does the Dawson County landscape mean for a house sale?
sections.html:
Dawson County sits in the Blue Ridge foothills and counts as part of metro Atlanta. Dawsonville holds the courthouse and is the only city. Juno and Afton are unincorporated. The land covers about 211 square miles, with ridges along the northern and western edges that reach roughly 3,500 feet.

Part of Lake Lanier lies in the southeast corner, and the Chestatee and Etowah rivers cross the county. Amicalola Falls, which drops 729 feet, is the tallest cascading waterfall east of the Mississippi and one of Georgia's Seven Natural Wonders. Black Mountain, at 3,600 feet, is the highest point. Fannin, Lumpkin, Hall, Forsyth, Cherokee, Pickens and Gilmer counties surround it, and part of the Chattahoochee National Forest falls inside the county line.

Lawmakers formed the county in December 1857 from parts of Gilmer and Lumpkin. It later became known for stock car racing, tied to moonshine runs on State Route 9, called Thunder Road, and a festival celebrates that history each October. Lake and mountain views, forest edges and slopes all change how a house is valued, so read your assessment notice with those features in mind.

sections.h2: How fast is Dawson County growing and what do houses cost?
sections.html:
Dawson County is the fastest-growing of the four Georgia counties in the Census Bureau's side-by-side QuickFacts table. The 2020 count of 26,798 rose to an estimated 35,365 by July 2025, an increase of 32.0 percent from the 2020 base.

  • Value of the typical owned home in the 2020 to 2024 survey: $406,700, over double any other county in the table.
  • Typical monthly rent: $1,626.
  • Housing units: 14,876, and 11,573 households.
  • Share of homes lived in by owners: 78.7 percent.
  • Households earning at the midpoint: $92,991 a year.
  • Building permits in 2025: 1,069, against 135 in Decatur County.
  • Residents 25 and older holding a four-year degree: 36.4 percent.

With values like these, the 40 percent assessment on a Dawson County house is a large base. A seller can use the tax estimator on the assessor's site to answer buyers' questions about yearly tax from the county's own tool.

sections.h2: Which special assessment programs does Dawson County offer?
sections.html:
Dawson County's assessor describes several programs that reduce the value taxed. Most need a 10-year covenant and an application between January 1 and April 1.

Dawson County special assessment programs (source: Dawson County Tax Assessor FAQ)
ProgramWhat the county says
Preferential agriculturalBona fide farm property assessed at 30 percent of fair market value instead of 40 percent, 10-year commitment
Conservation useAssessed at current use value, 10-year commitment, savings that can top 50 percent in some cases
Environmentally sensitiveCurrent use value for land kept natural and meeting Department of Natural Resources rules, 10 years
Residential transitionalCurrent use value for homes in areas shifting to other uses, 10-year covenant
TimberStanding timber untaxed until sold or harvested, then taxed at 100 percent of value
Equipment and fixturesAssessed at 40 percent of fair market value

Anyone selling acreage under one of these covenants should ask the assessor what happens to the covenant when ownership changes, because the county says the commitment runs for ten years.

sections.h2: When must Dawson County exemptions and returns be filed?
sections.html:
April 1 is the date that matters. Real property returns, personal property returns, conservation use and forest land applications, requests for parcel splits or combinations, and exemptions are all taken from January 1 through April 1. The assessor says no extension has been given for any type of exemption.

  • Regular homestead applications can be accepted year-round, but they must be in by April 1 to count for that tax year.
  • Senior and other specialized exemptions follow the same April 1 deadline.
  • Exemption applications are taken in person only.
  • After you receive an exemption, you do not reapply unless you move to another address.

Dawson County also publishes a list of assessment notices that came back undeliverable, as Georgia's O.C.G.A. 48-5-306(c) directs. If you changed addresses or inherited a parcel, check that list on the assessor's website so a missed notice does not cost you the appeal window.

sections.h2: How do I challenge a Dawson County valuation?
sections.html:
Appeals must be written and arrive within 45 days of the assessment notice. The county calls late ones invalid. Grounds are limited to taxability, uniformity with similar properties and value.

The assessors look at it first. When they leave the value alone, a three-person Board of Equalization named by the Grand Jury hears it. A taxpayer or the assessor who disagrees may then go to Superior Court.

Appeal volume has been unusually heavy. Under O.C.G.A. 48-5-311, a county where appeals reach 3 percent of parcels, or 3 percent of the digest's value, gets an extra 180 days to decide them. The assessor's page states that Dawson County crossed that threshold on June 7, 2024. Field appraisers handling appeals and reviews carry photo identification and drive marked county vehicles, and the county asks owners with questions to call (706) 344-3590.

sections.h2: How is the tax calculated in Dawson County?
sections.html:
The assessor's FAQ explains that the levy applies to 40 percent of fair market value, fixed at the start of each year. Millage is set annually. The county defines a mill as a dollar of tax for each $1,000 of assessed value. Property tax pays for police and fire services, schools, roads, bridges, water and parks, according to the county.

Fair market value means the amount a knowledgeable buyer would pay and a willing seller would accept in an arm's-length sale. The assessors use cost, market and income approaches. The market approach compares sales of similar properties, which is why a run of high-priced sales on your road tends to push your value up.

Ask the Dawson County tax commissioner for the millage that applies to your address, and use the assessor's estimator to test a number before you compare it with the bill.

sections.h2: What should a Dawson County seller do about the tax bill?
sections.html:
Request the balance from the tax commissioner before the sale contract is final. The county's FAQ says tax is charged to the owner on January 1, so a seller who closes later in the year may hold that year's bill. Write the split into the contract.

  • Mobile home bills carry their own date. The commissioner's site shows the 2026 mobile home bills were due April 1.
  • Payment options include the counter at Suite 1222 and the pay-by-phone line, (706) 701-2576.
  • If the house is under a conservation or agricultural covenant, tell the buyer and the assessor.
  • If an estate is selling, ask the assessor what documents are needed to update the owner and the homestead record.

Whoever the buyer is, obtain the payoff in writing and route it through the settlement agent.

faqs.q: Where is the Dawson County tax commissioner's office?
faqs.a: At 25 Justice Way, Suite 1222, inside the courthouse in downtown Dawsonville. Staff answer weekdays from eight to five at (706) 344-3520.

faqs.q: Can I pay my Dawson County property tax by phone?
faqs.a: Yes. The commissioner's website lists (706) 701-2576 for paying property tax by phone. You can also call the main office at (706) 344-3520 or pay at the counter.

faqs.q: What is the filing deadline for a Dawson County homestead exemption?
faqs.a: April 1. Regular homestead applications can be taken year-round, but one that arrives after April 1 does not count for that tax year, and applications must be made in person.

faqs.q: What is the Dawson County appeal period?
faqs.a: Forty-five days after the assessment notice arrives, and the appeal must be written. Late filings are invalid, per the county.

faqs.q: Is Dawson County property expensive compared with nearby Georgia counties?
faqs.a: Yes. The survey value for a typical owned home is $406,700 here, against $164,100 in Crawford, $140,200 in Crisp and $158,800 in Decatur.
